messages.author: c431c5b9ed1ca911
messages.subject: p 9 of "Qual. Comp. Analysis Using R"
parts:
Hi all

I was surprised to read here that "QCA is suited for addressing "causes of an effect" types of questions that ask for the reasons why a certain phenomena occur, rather than "effects of causes" questions that ask for the effects of a specific variable on the outcome" (my underlining)

My impression was that set relations are agnostic about time...so both kinds of analyses could be done using a set theory perspective, if you reread "effects of causes" as "effects of a cause"

With a "effects of a cause" analysis the effects would be conditions and the cause would be what normally/previously be called the "outcome" of interest. You would be looking to find what combinations of effects were most strongly associated with a particular cause. 

What have I misunderstood?
If correct ,can you name any published papers of this kind of analysis

.regards, rick davies

messages.subject: Re: [QCA] p 9 of "Qual. Comp. Analysis Using R"
parts:
Hi Rick

I think you are right that set-methods can be both - cause of effect and effect of cause-oriented. The sentences you quote, however, are statements about QCA. With its truth table analysis, QCA aims at covering as much of the outcome as possible, 'whatever it takes', to cite Mario Draghi, ie with as many disjunctions as possible. 
Does this make sense?

Best wishes
Carsten

messages.author: f782cba1fea3584e
messages.subject: Re: [QCA] p 9 of "Qual. Comp. Analysis Using R"
parts:
Dear Rick

A good summary of the different approaches to explanation can be found here
https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/abs/tale-of-two-cultures-contrasting-quantitative-and-qualitative-research/74CDE90B427798F4986F0B5039D48C67

Given its focus on causal complexity and set relations, QCA is generally not a good methods for assessing the specific effects of a (single) cause, or the size of that effect.

Hope this makes sense!
Best wishes
Eva
